payload.rationale: Observed facts: on September 16, 2026 the FOMC unanimously raised the target range 25bp to 3.75–4.00%, citing solid activity and elevated inflation (PCE 3.7%, core 3.4% projected for 2026). The September SEP median end-2026 midpoint of 4.1% implies roughly one additional 25bp hike across the two remaining meetings (October 28 and December), with the participant range spanning no further hikes (3.9%) to two more (4.4%). This makes a cut essentially off the table, so the question is hold versus hike in October. A one-hike-over-two-meetings median gives no clear signal on timing; a unanimous hike with inflation well above target argues for momentum toward back-to-back moves, while the Fed's frequent preference to pause and assess data after a move, and the median implying only one more step, argues for waiting until December. I weigh these roughly evenly. Too high risk: the unanimity and elevated inflation could signal a committee in an active tightening phase where consecutive hikes are the default, making October a hike (~55%+). Too low risk: many committees pace hikes after initiating, and a single remaining median hike is often deferred to the final meeting with new SEP; a soft data print or financial-stress episode before October 28 would also favor a hold. The cancelled-meeting clause adds negligible upside to YES. Overall ~50%.
limitations: No data available on intermeeting speeches, market-implied pricing (excluded by rules), or September/October inflation and labor releases.
SEP medians are year-end conditional judgments and do not identify the meeting for any adjustment.
Small evidence packet; the policy context leading to the September hike (prior cuts, shocks) is not described.
